input: Research pickling and preserving techniques for summer veg

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Summer veg is broad — knowing which specific vegetables (e.g. courgettes, cucumbers, tomatoes, peppers, green beans) narrows which techniques are actually relevant and worth researching.
Whether this is for personal home use, a family, or a wider audience (e.g. a blog or community group) changes the scale, tone, and depth of research needed.
There are many preservation methods — water-bath canning, fermentation, quick pickling, freezing, dehydrating — knowing which the user is drawn to or wants to focus on avoids wasted research effort.
Available equipment (e.g. a canning kit, fermentation crocks, a dehydrator) is a hard limit on which techniques are actually viable for this person.
Whether the research feeds into an imminent harvest glut or is general advance planning affects how urgently actionable the output needs to be.
The user may want a quick technique overview, a curated list of trusted recipes, a step-by-step guide, or notes comparing methods — this determines what a good research output actually looks like.
Knowing where the research will be captured (a notebook, a doc, a recipe app, a spreadsheet) shapes how it should be organised and what the immediate first action is.

gold.taskTitle: Research pickling and preserving summer vegetables
gold.taskDescription: Research pickling and preserving techniques suitable for summer vegetables, with the goal of building knowledge or producing a usable reference.

questions.title: Which specific vegetables are you planning to preserve?
questions.description: Identify the exact vegetables in scope (e.g. cucumbers, courgettes, tomatoes, peppers, green beans) so research stays focused on relevant techniques.

questions.title: Who are you preserving for — just yourself or others?
questions.description: Clarify whether this is for personal use, a household, or a wider group, as this affects the scale and depth of research required.

questions.title: Which preservation methods interest you most right now?
questions.description: Determine whether the user wants to focus on a specific method such as quick pickling, fermentation, water-bath canning, or dehydrating, rather than researching all methods equally.

questions.title: What equipment do you already have at home?
questions.description: Establish hard limits based on available tools (e.g. canning jars and lids, a preserving pan, fermentation weights, a dehydrator) to rule out impractical techniques.

questions.title: Is there a harvest or glut coming up soon, or is this advance planning?
questions.description: Understand the urgency — an imminent surplus means the output needs to be immediately actionable, while advance planning allows for more thorough, leisurely research.

questions.title: What does a useful research output look like to you?
questions.description: Clarify the desired deliverable — a quick technique comparison, a curated set of tested recipes, a detailed step-by-step guide, or a safety-focused reference — so the research has a clear end point.

questions.title: Where will you record and store what you find?
questions.description: Identify the tool or format for capturing research (e.g. a notebook, Google Doc, recipe app, printed folder) to determine how to organise notes and what the first concrete action step should be.
